shortAnswer: A DDoS attack overwhelms the service with traffic from many sources. Defence is layered: a CDN or WAF and rate limiting at the edge absorb most of it, and the application adds timeouts, connection limits, and cheap rejection of bad requests so legitimate traffic still gets through.
tips: Stress the layering: edge first, application second.
Name a concrete limiter for expensive endpoints.
title: Defending a Spring Boot application against DDoS attacks

commonMistakes: Forgetting RUNTIME retention, so nothing can read the annotation.
Expecting the annotation to execute code by itself.
detailedAnswer: An annotation is declared with @interface and its elements look like methods with defaults: @interface LogExecutionTime { boolean enabled() default true; }. Two meta-annotations matter: @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME), without which nothing can read it at runtime, and @Target, which restricts where it may be placed, for example ElementType.METHOD. The annotation itself does nothing; something must read it. The common patterns are an Aspect with a @Around pointcut matching @annotation(LogExecutionTime), which logs timing without touching business code, and a BeanPostProcessor that inspects beans at startup, for example to register methods as handlers. A frequent mistake is putting the annotation on a method that is called from inside the same class: the AOP proxy is bypassed, so the advice never runs, exactly as with @Transactional. Keep annotations for cross-cutting metadata, not for business rules that belong in code.
followUps: Why does the annotation do nothing on its own?
Why would an annotation on a self-invoked method never trigger?
question: How do you create and use a custom annotation in Spring Boot?
shortAnswer: Declare it with @interface, give it RUNTIME retention and a @Target, then process it: either with Spring AOP for behaviour such as logging, or by reading it at startup with reflection or a BeanPostProcessor.
tips: Give the three parts: declare, retain at runtime, process it.
Mention the self-invocation proxy trap.
title: Creating a custom annotation in Spring Boot

commonMistakes: Declaring success because the deploy job went green.
Watching averages instead of percentiles.
detailedAnswer: A successful deploy is not a successful release. The verification sequence is: first, confirm the new instances are actually serving traffic, through health and readiness endpoints and load balancer registration; second, run a small set of smoke tests that exercise the critical paths, login, the main API calls, and the payment flow, against production; third, watch the metrics that matter for at least one business cycle, comparing error rate, latency percentiles, and saturation against the pre-deploy baseline, because averages hide regressions that p99 reveals. Set explicit rollback triggers before the deploy, for example error rate above 1% for five minutes, and make sure the rollback is a single action, not a rebuild. Feature flags make this safer still: the code ships dark, the flag is enabled for a small percentage, and the blast radius stays small if the verification fails.
followUps: Why is p99 more useful than the average latency here?
What makes a rollback trigger explicit rather than a gut feeling?
question: Scenario: you have just deployed a new version to production. How do you verify it is healthy before declaring success?
shortAnswer: Check health endpoints and error rates, run smoke tests against real traffic paths, compare key metrics with the pre-deploy baseline, and keep the rollback ready with a clear trigger; do not declare success because the deploy finished.
tips: Separate 'deploy finished' from 'release healthy'.
Name the rollback trigger as a number, not a feeling.
title: Scenario: verifying a deployment in production

commonMistakes: Testing everything with @SpringBootTest and a slow suite nobody runs.
Using an in-memory database that behaves differently from production.
detailedAnswer: The pyramid exists because each layer has a different cost. Unit tests for services and domain logic are fast and precise, and they should be the majority. Slice tests use Spring's test slices: @WebMvcTest for controllers with mocked services, and @DataJpaTest for repositories against an in-memory or container database, which test the layer's real wiring without starting the whole application. Full @SpringBootTest tests are the slowest and most brittle, so reserve them for the paths that genuinely need the whole context, such as startup configuration and security. For anything that touches a real database, queue, or external service, Testcontainers gives you the real dependency in a container, which removes a whole class of 'works on my machine' failures. At service boundaries, contract tests verify that a provider still honours what its consumers expect, which is cheaper than end-to-end tests and catches the breaking change at the source.
followUps: Why are slice tests preferable to @SpringBootTest for a controller?
What problem do Testcontainers solve that an in-memory database does not?
question: What testing strategy do you recommend for a Spring Boot application?
shortAnswer: Follow the test pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer slice tests for the web and data layers, and a small number of full integration tests with Testcontainers, with contract tests at service boundaries.
tips: Structure the answer as the pyramid, bottom to top.
Name one slice annotation per layer.
title: Testing strategy for a Spring Boot application

commonMistakes: Renaming a column in the same release as the code change.
Running a locking migration against a live table.
detailedAnswer: The problem is that the old and new versions of the application run side by side during a rolling deploy, so the schema must work for both. Expand-and-contract solves this in three releases. First, expand: add the new column as nullable, or add the new table, in a migration that changes nothing the old code depends on. Second, deploy the new code that writes to both the old and the new shape and reads from the new one. Third, contract: once the old code is gone, drop the old column or table in a separate release. The traps are renames and type changes, which break the old code immediately, and long-running migrations that lock the table, such as adding a column with a default on a huge table or building an index without CONCURRENTLY in Postgres. Flyway or Liquibase version the migrations, but they do not make an unsafe migration safe: the safety comes from the pattern and from testing the migration against a production-sized copy first.
followUps: Why must a column rename be done in two releases?
What makes a migration lock a table, and how do you avoid it?
question: How do you change a production database schema without downtime?
shortAnswer: Use the expand-and-contract pattern: first deploy a backward-compatible change that both old and new code tolerate, then deploy the new code, then remove the old shape in a later release; never run a locking migration against a live table.
tips: Walk the three phases in order.
Name the rename as the classic breaking change.
title: Zero-downtime database migrations

commonMistakes: Using field injection because it is shorter.
Reaching for the ApplicationContext in application code.
detailedAnswer: Field injection with @Autowired on a private field is the most common form in tutorials and the worst in production: the dependencies are invisible in the constructor, the fields cannot be final, the class cannot be instantiated in a plain unit test without reflection, and the container must use reflection to set them. Constructor injection fixes all of that: the dependencies are explicit parameters, the fields are final, and a test constructs the object with new. Since Spring 4.3, a single constructor is autowired automatically, so no annotation is needed. For the cases field injection seems to solve, there are better tools: @Bean methods in a @Configuration class for wiring third-party classes, ObjectProvider<T> when a dependency is optional or should be resolved lazily, and @Lookup for prototype beans. Getting a bean from the ApplicationContext directly works but hides the dependency and couples the code to the container, so treat it as a last resort for framework code, not application code.
followUps: How do you inject an optional dependency without field injection?
Why can a constructor-injected class be tested without Spring?
question: What are the alternatives to @Autowired, and why is field injection discouraged?
shortAnswer: Prefer constructor injection, which needs no annotation on a single constructor and makes dependencies explicit and immutable; other options are @Bean methods, ObjectProvider for optional or lazy dependencies, and direct ApplicationContext lookups, which should be a last resort.
tips: Lead with the testability argument; it is the strongest one.
Mention that a single constructor needs no annotation.
title: Alternatives to @Autowired field injection

commonMistakes: Making downstream calls with no timeout.
Retrying without backoff or a limit.
detailedAnswer: RestTemplate is the old blocking client: simple and familiar, but each call holds a thread, and it is in maintenance mode, so no new features are coming. WebClient is its replacement: non-blocking and reactive, so one thread can serve many in-flight calls, which matters when a service fans out to several others. Feign is declarative: you write an interface with annotations, and Spring Cloud generates the client, including load balancing and, with Resilience4j, a circuit breaker. The client choice is less important than the resilience around it: every call needs a connection timeout and a read timeout, or a slow downstream will exhaust your thread pool; retries need backoff and a limit, or they amplify an outage; a circuit breaker stops calls to a service that is already down; and a correlation id must be propagated in headers, or a request cannot be traced across services. A call without a timeout is the most common production failure in this area.
followUps: Why is a call without a timeout so dangerous?
When would you choose WebClient over Feign?
question: How should one microservice call another, and how do RestTemplate, WebClient, and Feign differ?
shortAnswer: Use a declarative client such as Feign or a non-blocking WebClient for new code; RestTemplate is blocking and in maintenance mode. Whichever you pick, add timeouts, retries with backoff, a circuit breaker, and propagate correlation ids.
tips: Compare the three clients in one pass, then pivot to resilience.
Name the timeout as the most common production failure.
title: Service-to-service calls: RestTemplate, WebClient, and Feign

commonMistakes: Deciding by seniority instead of by criteria.
Letting the argument run until the sprint fails.
detailedAnswer: The lead's job is not to pick the cleverer design; it is to unblock the team. Start by listening to each person separately, because in a group argument people defend positions rather than explaining reasoning. Then reframe the disagreement around criteria the team can agree on: what does each option cost in complexity, risk, and time, and what does the decision need to be reversible or not. If the decision is easily reversible, decide fast and revisit later; if it is hard to reverse, spend the time to prototype or spike the risky part. Make the decision explicit, name who owns it, write down the reasoning and the trade-offs, and set a date to revisit it if the assumptions change. What the lead must not do is decide by seniority, let the argument run until the sprint fails, or pretend a compromise that satisfies nobody is a decision. A team that sees decisions made cleanly and revisited honestly will argue less the next time.
followUps: How do you decide when a technical disagreement needs a prototype?
What do you do if the same disagreement keeps coming back?
question: Scenario: two developers on your team disagree strongly about a technical approach and the argument is blocking the sprint. As the lead, what do you do?
shortAnswer: Separate the people from the problem: hear each side privately, agree on the decision criteria and who decides, make a decision with a time-box for revisiting it, and document it so the team can move on without relitigating it.
tips: Give the sequence: listen separately, agree criteria, decide, document.
Distinguish reversible from irreversible decisions.
title: Scenario: handling conflict within your team as a lead

commonMistakes: Cutting testing to meet the date.
Accepting every new request after the plan is set.
detailedAnswer: The first step is to make the work visible: list everything, estimate it honestly, and sort by the value delivered and the risk of not doing it, not by who shouted loudest. Then cut scope, not quality: a smaller feature that works is worth more than a larger one shipped broken, and quality cuts become production incidents that cost more than the time saved. Present the choice to stakeholders as options with consequences, for example 'we can ship X and Y by Friday, or X, Y, and Z two weeks later', because a trade-off presented as options gets a decision, while a complaint about workload gets sympathy and no decision. Once the plan is agreed, freeze it: every new request goes through the same ranking, or the team spends the sprint re-planning instead of building. Finally, say what is being dropped out loud, in writing, so nobody is surprised at the deadline, and protect the team's focus by being the person who says no.
followUps: How do you present a scope cut to stakeholders so it gets accepted?
When is it right to push back on a deadline instead of cutting scope?
question: Scenario: your team has more work than it can finish before a hard deadline. How do you prioritise?
shortAnswer: Rank by business impact and risk, cut scope before cutting quality, make the trade-off visible to stakeholders with options rather than a single plea for more time, and protect the team from thrash by freezing the plan once it is set.
tips: Give the options-with-consequences framing.
Mention freezing the plan after the decision.
title: Scenario: prioritising work under tight deadlines and limited resources

commonMistakes: Starting a big-bang rewrite with no tests.
Refactoring code nobody needs to change.
detailedAnswer: A big-bang rewrite is the classic trap: it takes months, the new system must reproduce undocumented behaviour the old one accumulated, and the business gets nothing until the end. The safer approach starts with understanding: read the code, talk to the people who run it, and find the seams where it can be tested. Then add characterization tests, tests that capture what the code actually does today, not what it should do, around the area you are about to change, so a change that breaks behaviour is caught immediately. Change incrementally, leaving each area slightly better than you found it, and use the strangler pattern for larger pieces: route new behaviour through new code while the old code keeps serving the rest. Rewrite only the piece you can prove is cheaper to replace than to fix, and only when a business change gives you the reason and the budget.
followUps: What is a characterization test, and how is it different from a unit test?
When is a rewrite actually the right call?
question: Scenario: you inherit a large legacy codebase with no tests and fragile behaviour. What is your approach?
shortAnswer: Do not rewrite it: first make it safe to change with characterization tests around the code you must touch, then improve it incrementally with the boy-scout rule, and extract or replace pieces only when a business change forces you to.
tips: Lead with 'do not rewrite it'; it is the expected judgement.
Explain characterization tests as the safety net.
title: Scenario: taking over a legacy codebase

commonMistakes: Logging personal data in plain text.
Storing data you do not need 'just in case'.
detailedAnswer: Privacy is a design concern, not a checkbox at the end. Start with minimisation: collect only the data the feature needs, and do not store what you do not need, because data you do not hold cannot leak. Protect what you keep: TLS in transit, encryption at rest for sensitive fields, and secrets in a vault rather than in configuration or code. Restrict access by role and by need, and audit who accessed what, because most breaches involve legitimate access used wrongly. Keep personal data out of logs and error messages, where it is routinely copied into systems with weaker controls, and mask it in non-production environments. Know the rules that apply: retention periods, the right to deletion, and consent requirements under regulations such as GDPR and India's DPDP Act, and design the deletion path before launch, because deleting a user's data from backups, caches, and analytics is the part teams forget until a request arrives.
followUps: Why is data minimisation the strongest privacy control?
How do you handle a user's deletion request across backups and caches?
question: Scenario: your service handles personal data. How do you handle privacy and security as a senior developer?
shortAnswer: Minimise what you collect, encrypt sensitive data in transit and at rest, restrict access to the minimum needed, keep personal data out of logs, and know the retention and deletion rules that apply to your users.
tips: Start with minimisation; it frames everything else.
Mention logs as the place personal data leaks most often.
title: Scenario: handling data privacy and security in your projects
